_comment: Russian folk tales cut from Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), Project Gutenberg #50011. All passages paraphrase.

title.en: The Three Kingdoms: Copper, Silver, and Gold

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於莫斯科）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Three Kingdoms'

summary.en: The youngest prince follows a golden falcon into three kingdoms of copper, silver, and gold, wins the prisoner princesses, and must descend into a well to rescue his brothers who have lowered him into the otherworld and abandoned him there.
summary.zh: 幼王子隨金獵鷹入銅銀金三國，救出被囚之三位公主；然其兄將他繫入冥井棄之，他須自尋歸路復救兄返。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale (ATU-type descent to the underground kingdom); standard collection.

passages.text: A tsar's three sons, hunting, rouse a golden falcon that carries off their father's horse; the youngest follows it through forests until he reaches the copper kingdom, where a princess taken by the falcon gives him a ball of thread that rolls ahead, showing the way. Kingdom by kingdom — copper, silver, gold — he finds a princess and a way onward, each telling him the falcon is to reach its father's house at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Three Kingdoms'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He rescues all three princesses, and the brothers who waited above lower him into the well to the golden princess — then cut the rope and leave him below, taking the maidens home. In the underworld he is helped by a griffin (or eagle) that carries him up over the sea, fed by the carcasses he throws to it from his own flesh; the last bite he cuts from himself and heals at the golden princess's well. Returning, he exposes his brothers and marries the golden princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Three Kingdoms'; not verbatim.

title.en: Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf
title.zh: 伊萬沙皇子、火鳥與灰狼

region.en: Russian fairyland, garden of the Fire-Bird (symbolic pin at Moscow)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，火鳥之園（象徵性定位於莫斯科）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf'

summary.en: Ivan Tsarevich is caught by the gray wolf for stealing the Fire-Bird, and must go on to steal the golden-maned horse of King Afron and the princess Yelena the Fair; his brothers murder him for the treasures — but the wolf brings back the water of death and water of life, and Ivan lives.
summary.zh: 伊萬沙皇子竊火鳥被灰狼擒，又受命去竊阿弗隆王之金鬃馬與美人葉連娜公主；其兄為奪寶而弒之——灰狼銜來死水與活水，伊萬復生。

passages.text: The Fire-Bird came nightly to the tsar's garden and ate the golden apples; whoever caught it should win the kingdom. The eldest son watched and slept; the second watched and slept; the youngest, Ivan, caught one fiery feather — then, spurred by his brothers, sat up all the third night and seized the bird itself. But the brothers grew weary on the road, slept, and Ivan was caught by the gray wolf, who devoured the horse but, knowing who he was, spared the prince and promised to serve him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The wolf changed itself into the horse of King Afron to trick that king into giving up the golden-maned steed, and again into a golden carriage to rescue Princess Yelena the Fair, who fell in love with Ivan on the road. At the end of the journey the brothers murdered Ivan, cut him to pieces, and rode home with the treasures.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gray wolf gathered a raven's nest and forced the old raven to bring the water of death and the water of life; the dead water gathered the torn body together and the living water brought Ivan to life again. The wolf took the raven shape of the brothers' shame and Ivan came home ahead of them, to tell his father all — the treacherous brothers were punished, and Ivan married Yelena the Fair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: The Feather of Bright Finist the Falcon
title.zh: 明亮獵鷹菲尼斯特之羽

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於斯摩棱斯克）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Feather of Bright Finist the Falcon'

summary.en: The youngest daughter buys a magic feather that becomes the falcon-hero Finist by night; her jealous sisters stab the falcon in his sleep, and the girl must wear out three pairs of iron shoes and beg at three women's doors before she can wake him with her tears.
summary.zh: 幼女購得神羽，夜間化為獵鷹英雄菲尼斯特；嫉妒的姐姐趁其睡時刺傷獵鷹；少女乃磨破三雙鐵鞋、三度叩三女之門，以淚水喚醒他。

sensitivity.note: Classic Russian fairy tale (Cinderella-type with bride quest in reverse).

passages.text: The youngest of three sisters bought at the market a feather of bright Finist the falcon. At night she opened the box, and out came a falcon that became a handsome young man; by day he flew away, by night he came again, and the girl loved him. Her jealous sisters learned of the youth, and while he slept they stuck needles and knives into his feathered coat, so that when the falcon flew up in the morning the iron had cut him, and he beat against the walls and vanished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Feather of Bright Finist the Falcon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl set out to find him in three pairs of iron shoes and three iron staffs, which she wore out; she came to three old women in turn — one gave her a golden distaff, one a silver, one a golden spindle — and learned that Finist was bewitched into the Tsar's son and served by a false princess. She traded her gold and silver spinning gifts for three nights at his bedside, weeping until the third night, when her tears fell on the prince's shoulder and burned him, and he woke and knew her — for he had dreamed of her and never dreamed of the false bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: The Water of Death and the Water of Life

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於梁贊）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Water of Youth, Water of Life, and Water of Death'

summary.en: Sent to fetch the waters of death and life for a blind or wounded tsar, the hero drinks the water of youth, is flung from a ship by treacherous brothers, is picked up by merchants, and returns — where the dead water and the living water sort the innocent from the guilty.
summary.zh: 為失明或重傷之沙皇取死水與活水，英雄途中飲青春之水，為奸兄拋入海中，為商船所救，終返——死水活水自會辨忠奸。

passages.text: A tsar grown old and blind is told that only the waters of life, death, and youth can cure him; his sons set out after them. The youngest, misled and mocked by his brothers, finds the waters in the world beyond a mountain of glass — the dead water to gather a broken body, the living water to make it breathe, the water of youth to make it young.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Water of Youth, Water of Life, and Water of Death'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His brothers fling him into the sea with a stone to drown him and carry the false waters home; the youngest is picked up by merchants and comes back as a stranger to his own court. There the truth is proved by ordeal: the guilty are struck by the water of death and the innocent live. The blind tsar's eyes are washed with the true waters and he sees again; the traitors are punished and the youngest son inherits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: Koshchei Without-Death: The Needle in the Egg

region.en: Russian fairyland, island of Buyan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，布揚島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Koshchei Without-Death'

summary.en: Koshchei the Deathless carries his life hidden: in an egg, in a duck, in a hare, in a chest, on the island of Buyan — and only when the hunter breaks the egg and crushes the needle does the wizard's death arrive at last.
summary.zh: 不死之科謝伊藏其命於蛋中，蛋在鴨腹，鴨在兔腹，兔在箱中，箱在布揚島——唯獵手破蛋搗針，巫師之死方至。

sensitivity.note: Classic external-soul tale (parallel to Jack-and-the-Giant and Mwindo); cluster-tagged.

passages.text: Koshchei Without-Death cannot be killed, for his death is not in his body: it lies in an egg, the egg in a duck, the duck in a hare, the hare in a chest, and the chest stands on the island of Buyan under an oak — so the tales say. Whatever villainy he does, no sword can find him, for a man who holds his death elsewhere cannot be reached by weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Koshchei Without-Death'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In Curtin's telling a princess — Vassilissa Golden Tress — is stolen by the wizard; the hero follows on horseback, is shattered and remade by friendly animals, and at last rides the hare down, opens the chest, and takes the egg in his hand. The wizard trembles, holds him by the hair, and begs — but the hunter breaks the egg, crushes the needle within, and Koshchei's death comes upon him at once; the stolen princesses are freed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.zh: 金辮瓦西麗莎：不蒙頭之美

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於弗拉基米爾）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Vassilissa Golden Tress, Bareheaded Beauty'

summary.en: Bareheaded beauty — whose uncovered hair shames a whole court — is stolen by Koshchei, and won back by the youngest huntsman whom her golden hair has cured of blindness.
summary.zh: 不蒙頭之美——其散髮羞煞滿朝——為科謝伊所竊；被她金髮治癒眼盲之幼獵手終將她救回。

passages.text: The tsar's general searches the land for the bareheaded beauty, Vassilissa Golden Tress, whose uncovered hair outshines every veiled head. Found and hidden, she is stolen by Koshchei the Deathless; her beauty is so strong that the tsar who would marry her is blinded by it, and only she herself can cure him — which is why the wizard carries her off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Vassilissa Golden Tress, Bareheaded Beauty'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The youngest huntsman of the blind tsar is cured when her hair touches his eyes, and he rides alone through the forest, sleeps in the dragon-lair, is remade by the animals he spared, and wins the egg of Koshchei's death; crushing the needle, he frees the princess, and Vassilissa opens her hair to the light and is bareheaded no more by any man's command.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

region.en: Russian fairyland (symbolic pin at Nizhny Novgorod)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於下諾夫哥羅德）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Ring with Twelve Screws'

summary.en: A dying fisherman's son finds a ring shut with twelve screws; at midnight his dead father rises and tells him how to open it — and each screw released brings a wizard's servant and a fortune, until the twelfth brings the one the ring's true owner fears.
summary.zh: 瀕死漁夫之子得一枚十二道螺紋封閉的戒指；午夜亡父顯靈告其開法——每擰開一道，即召來一名精靈僕從與一份財富，直到第十二道引來戒指真正主人所懼者。

passages.text: A fisherman's family is starving; the son nets a great fish and spares it, and is rewarded with a small ring shut with twelve screws. His dying father warns him: never open the ring by day. At midnight the father appears and teaches him to unloose the screws one by one, each releasing a spirit of the ring's service — gold, grain, ships, palaces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Ring with Twelve Screws'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the twelfth screw holds the master of the ring's first wife — a giant's widow with iron teeth — who seizes the youth and flies away with him to the world's end; the youth escapes by calling each released spirit back to serve him, and the twelve servants together pull the ring's fortunes back from the widow's iron grip, so that he comes home with the princess and the ring closed forever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於特維爾）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Seven Simeons, Full Brothers'

summary.en: Seven brothers each with one miraculous gift — a super-sighted eye, a stealer, a builder of a tower to heaven, a swift runner, a shooter, a fisher — use their gifts together to steal the tsar's famous beauty Helen, escape the fastest ship of the tsar by building an island of gold, and win pardon and riches.
summary.zh: 七兄弟各有一項神技——千里眼、妙手、造塔通天、疾行、神射、善漁——合力競技，偷取沙皇傾城美人海倫，以金島誘開追艦，得赦而富貴。

passages.text: Seven brothers, full brothers, Simeons by name, each have one gift: the first sees a hundred versts with a single eye; the second can steal like a mouse; the third can build a tower to the sky; the fourth runs like the wind; the fifth shoots with unerring aim; the sixth catches fish with his bare hands. Each gift alone seems useless to the tsar, but together they are a kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Seven Simeons, Full Brothers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They use them to steal the famous beauty Helen from the tsar himself: the watchful eye finds her ship, the thief takes her aboard unseen, the tower-builder raises the tower to carry them over the sea, the runner carries the boat, the shooter clears the way, the fisher finds the road under the water. Pursued by the tsar's fleet, they build an island of gold in the middle of the sea where the pursuers' ships founder, and the tsar, finding his Helen wedded and beyond reach, laughs instead of hanging them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於蘇茲達爾）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Enchanted Princess'

summary.en: The hero must break an enchantment without a word spoken or a forbidden thing touched — and the smallest slip destroys everything, until a true silence of three days wins the princess and the castle.
summary.zh: 英雄須在不言一語、不犯一戒之下破除魔法——稍有失誤便前功盡棄；唯三日的真正靜默方能贏得公主與城堡。

passages.text: A youth finds a palace of the enchanted princess where every servant is marble and everything lies under a spell. He is warned: he may take what he likes, but he must not speak a word nor touch what is forbidden; if he keeps the rule for three days the enchantment will break, but at the least slip everything turns to stone again and the princess is lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Enchanted Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the third night a fly torments him, a candle falls, and almost he speaks; but the true silence holds, the statues breathe, the princess wakes, and the whole court steps out of its spell. The youth marries the princess and rules the kingdom his silence bought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: Vassilissa the Cunning and the Tsar of the Sea
title.zh: 機智的瓦西麗莎與海沙皇

region.en: Russian fairyland, sea kingdom (symbolic pin at Astrakhan)
region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境，海之王國（象徵性定位於阿斯特拉罕）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Vassilissa the Cunning, and the Tsar of the Sea'

summary.en: When the Tsar of the Sea drags an old merchant down for a debt of magic, his daughter Vassilissa teaches her mortal lover to outwit the sea-court with a silver and a golden dove, a spinning wheel of invisibility, and the riddle that saves his life three times.
summary.zh: 海沙皇因魔法債拖走老商人；其女瓦西麗莎以銀鴿金鴿、隱形紡車與三度救命之謎，教會凡人戀人智鬥海宮。

passages.text: An old merchant owes the Tsar of the Sea a debt of magic and is dragged down beneath the waters; his daughter Vassilissa is sent with him to learn what the sea-tsar wants. She meets the sea-tsar's daughter, the wise Vassilissa, who pities her and teaches her what the court demands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Vassilissa the Cunning, and the Tsar of the Sea'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The mortal hero who comes to the rescue is told by the sea-tsar's daughter to answer the riddle, spin the invisible wheel, and change into the silver dove and the golden one, so that the sea-tsar's three tests are each met. The lover is saved three times — by the daughter's cunning, by his own patience, and by the waters themselves, which bear him home. He marries her, and the sea's debt is paid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: The Footless and the Blind: Two Cripples Who Saved a Tsarevich
title.zh: 無足者與盲者：兩位殘者救回沙皇子

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於普斯科夫）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Footless and the Blind'

summary.en: A blind man and a man without feet are given to one another as if the tsar's joke — the blind one carries the footless one, who sees for them both; they find a cure for each other's disability at a witch's well, and together rescue the tsarevich.
summary.zh: 沙皇戲言令盲者與無足者相依——盲者背負無足者，無足者為其看路；他們在女巫之井找到互愈之水，合力救回沙皇子。

passages.text: The tsar jests that the blind man shall carry the man without feet, and each shall be the other's legs and eyes; the pair set out to seek their fortunes. The footless one sees a fire in the forest, a witch's well, and the herbs that cure blindness and lameness, and the blind one carries him to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Footless and the Blind'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Each is cured at the well and hears, in the witch's garden, the fate of the stolen tsarevich; they free him, bear him home, and the tsar's joke has made the two cripples into the heroes of his kingdom — the blind man's legs and the lame man's eyes being worth more together than the tsar's whole court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pig with Gold Bristles, the Deer with Golden Horns
title.zh: 金鬃豬、金角鹿與金尾金鬃駿馬

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於沃羅涅日）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'The Pig with Gold Bristles, the Deer with Golden Horns, and the Golden-Maned Steed'

summary.en: A father's dying command — to guard a garden of golden apples — is broken by the youngest son, who follows a golden pig, a golden-horned deer, and a golden-maned steed into the underworld garden of a many-headed dragon, and wins the girl there.
summary.zh: 父親臨終命幼子守護金蘋果園；幼子失職追尋金鬃豬、金角鹿、金尾金鬃駿馬，闖入多首龍之下界花園，贏得彼處少女。

passages.text: On his deathbed a father warns his sons that thieves will come for the golden apples in the garden: the pig with gold bristles, the deer with golden horns, the golden-maned steed with golden tail. The eldest watches and sleeps; the second watches and sleeps; the youngest shoots at the thief and follows the blood into a hill, down into a garden where the dragon keeps its treasures.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'The Pig with Gold Bristles, the Deer with Golden Horns, and the Golden-Maned Steed'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He takes the three wonders and the girl who tends the garden, and the dragon — a twelve-headed serpent riding its horse of fire — pursues; the girl's magic horse outstrips the serpent's, and the hero severs the serpent's heads and burns the body. The brothers take the treasures home; the youngest marries the garden's keeper, and the golden apples ripen again in the tsar's garden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.

title.en: Go to the Verge of Death and Split the Grain of Wood

region.zh: 俄羅斯童話之境（象徵性定位於卡盧加）

texts.period: Collected and translated by Jeremiah Curtin, 1890

source.work: Jeremiah Curtin, Myths and Folk-Tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars (1890), 'Go to the Verge of Death and Split the Grain of Wood'

summary.en: Sent for a cure that lies at 'the verge of death', the hero learns to split the grain of living wood — inside which his sisters' stolen souls lie hidden — and finds the many-headed dragon that keeps them.
summary.zh: 為求『死界』之藥而行的英雄，學會劈開活木之紋——妹妹們被竊的魂靈即藏其中——並尋獲看守她們的多首龍。

passages.text: A father lies dying and the cure is to be found 'at the verge of death, where the grain of wood must be split'; the youngest son goes alone, for the roads are deadly. He serves a witch who teaches him how to split wood — the grain of the forest — and finds in each split log a wonder his brothers laughed at.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890), 'Go to the Verge of Death and Split the Grain of Wood'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the verge of death he comes to the dragon's garden and finds his stolen sisters there; he slays the dragon with the axe-split of living wood, gathers the sisters, and brings them home so that the dying father rises from his bed — the cure of the verge of death is the dragon's own blood, split out of the grain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Curtin (1890); not verbatim.
